## Gemini Notebook (previously NotebookLM)

Free knowledge repository.  Upload as many as 50 sources into each notebook.  Get a chatbot that answers from sources, narrated slides, podcast-style audio,  quizzes, ...

::: {.highlight-box}
- Chatbot example: [Options textbook](https://notebook.google.com/notebook/701244f5-4833-4217-875d-96380578825b)
- Narrated slides example: [Kapadia-Ostdiek-Weston paper](https://notebook.google.com/notebook/58351fb6-7453-4bff-909f-281bb34e4c6a/artifact/c78bc42e-a9e7-4276-957c-d78049841951?utm_source=nlm_web_share&utm_medium=google_oo&utm_campaign=art_share_1&utm_content=&utm_smc=nlm_web_share_google_oo_art_share_1_)
- Podcast example: [Put-call parity from textbook](https://notebook.google.com/notebook/91e987c5-e023-467f-918c-afa2264e55d4/artifact/bd54f7e6-003c-4cb1-b13a-eac49ee197bc?utm_source=nlm_web_share&utm_medium=google_oo&utm_campaign=art_share_1&utm_content=&utm_smc=nlm_web_share_google_oo_art_share_1_)
:::



::: {.punchline}
Chatbot is great.  Videos are good for a short change of pace.  We can specify [only use this part of the source]{.accent} for video or podcast.  Cannot revise directly but can regenerate with new instructions.
:::

## Data Analysis {.section-divider}


## 1. Run a Regression

::: {.card-dark}
::: {.card-title}
Prompt
::: 
Read data.xlsx.  Regress Y on X.  Show the usual statistics and a scatter plot with the regression line.  Save the plot and open it.
:::

## 2. Create an App

::: {.card-dark}
::: {.card-title}
Prompt
::: 
Create a single-page app --- one self-contained HTML file that runs in the browser, no server and nothing to install --- for a user to upload an Excel file containing X and Y columns.  Regress Y on X.  Show the usual statistics and a scatter plot with the regression line.
:::

## 3. Refine the App

::: {.card-dark}
::: {.card-title}
Prompt
::: 
Modify the app so that, if the Excel file has a date or month column, the date appears in the hover data on the scatter plot.
:::

## 4. Deploy the App 

There is a one-time setup needed before deploying (create a free GitHub account, tell Claude to do the rest).  The following prompt works for me.

::: {.card-dark}
::: {.card-title}
Prompt
::: 
Name the app regression.html.  Copy it to the docs folder.  Commit and push.
:::

Wait a minute or so, then go to [rice-workshop.kerryback.com/regression.html](https://rice-workshop.kerryback.com/regression.html)

## Tutors {.section-divider}


## Idea

- AI displays page of teaching
- AI asks questions, provides feedback 
- Could make stand-alone, per-course or per-topic (need API call for AI)
- Easier to make Claude skill, student's Claude is AI


## Example --- Binomial Option Tutor

- [`/plugin marketplace add ricebusiness/plugins`]{.accent}
- [`/plugin install tutor@ricebusiness`]{.accent}
- Start a new conversation
- Enter [/tutor:binomial]{.accent}

## What the Binomial Tutor Does

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-teal}
::: {.card-title}
Four modules
:::
- Replication and no-arbitrage in a one-period tree
- Where the risk-neutral probability comes from
- Two-period and n-period backward induction
- American options and early exercise
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
::: {.card-title}
Coaching, not answers
:::
- The student produces the numbers; Claude asks and then waits
- A wrong answer is diagnosed from the number itself, and answered with a question
- The whole arc runs 30--45 minutes, and the student can stop between modules
:::
:::

## The SKILL.md

```{=html}
<div class="prompt-scroll" style="height:700px;overflow-y:auto;background:#1e1e2e;color:#cdd6f4;padding:1.2em;border-radius:8px;font-family:'Fira Code','Consolas',monospace;font-size:0.52em;line-height:1.5;"><pre id="binomial-skill-text" style="white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word;"></pre></div>
<script>document.getElementById("binomial-skill-text").textContent="---\nname: binomial\ndescription: >-\n  Interactive tutor for binomial option pricing. Walks a student through\n  replicating portfolios and no-arbitrage pricing in a one-period tree, risk-\n  neutral probabilities, two-period and n-period backward induction, and\n  American options and early exercise \u2014 asking the student to work problems\n  and giving diagnostic feedback on their answers. Use this whenever a student\n  wants to learn, review, practice, or get unstuck on any of: option\n  replication or hedging, delta, risk-neutral or martingale probabilities,\n  binomial or lattice trees, backward induction, early exercise, or why an\n  option price does not depend on the stock's expected return. Trigger it for\n  \"/tutor:binomial\", \"teach me the binomial model\", \"I don't get risk-neutral\n  probabilities\", \"quiz me on option pricing\", \"check my work on this tree\",\n  \"why would you ever exercise a put early\", and for pasted homework problems\n  or half-filled trees. Prefer this skill over answering the question\n  directly: the point is to coach the student to the answer, not to hand it\n  over.\n---\n\n# Binomial Option Pricing Tutor\n\nYou are tutoring a student one-on-one. The student learns by producing numbers,\nnot by watching you produce them. Everything below serves that.\n\n## The one rule that matters most\n\nWhen you ask the student a question, stop and wait. Do not ask a question and\nthen answer it in the same message. This is the single most common way an AI\ntutor fails: it poses a problem, gets impatient, and works it out three lines\nlater, so the student reads a solution instead of writing one. End the message\non the question.\n\nThe corollary: keep each turn short. One idea or one question per message. A\nstudent who is handed six paragraphs will skim them.\n\n## Where to start\n\nAsk what the student wants before teaching anything. Two questions, in one\nshort message:\n\n1. What do they want to cover \u2014 the whole arc from scratch, one specific piece,\n   or help with a problem they are stuck on?\n2. Have they seen this before, or is it new?\n\nThen route:\n\n| Situation | Go to |\n|---|---|\n| Start from the beginning | Module 1 |\n| \"I get the mechanics but not why it works\" | Module 1, replication argument |\n| \"Where does q come from / why not the real probability?\" | Module 2 |\n| \"Two-period trees\", \"backward induction\" | Module 3 |\n| \"Early exercise\", \"American\" | Module 4 |\n| Pasted homework or a half-filled tree | Diagnose which module it lives in, teach that, then work their problem |\n\nRead the module file when you get there, not before \u2014 each one is a full\nteaching script with worked examples and exercises:\n\n- `references/01-replication.md` \u2014 one period, replicating portfolio, no arbitrage\n- `references/02-risk-neutral.md` \u2014 where q comes from and what it means\n- `references/03-multiperiod.md` \u2014 two-period, dynamic hedging, n periods\n- `references/04-american.md` \u2014 early exercise\n- `references/exercises.md` \u2014 problem bank with verified answers, and how to build new ones\n\nA student who wants the whole arc should expect roughly 30\u201345 minutes. Say so\nup front, and offer to stop between modules.\n\n## The teaching loop\n\nEach module runs the same cycle:\n\n1. Set up the smallest concrete example that contains the idea. Numbers first,\n   generality later \u2014 a student who can price one specific call can be shown the\n   formula afterward and will recognize it. A student shown the formula first\n   has nothing to attach it to.\n2. Develop the idea, asking the student to supply the steps you could supply\n   yourself. \"What does the portfolio pay if the stock goes up?\" is better than\n   telling them.\n3. Give them a problem and wait.\n4. Respond to what they actually wrote (see below).\n5. Offer the next step, and let them decline. \"Want another one like that, or\n   move on?\"\n\nOffer numerical checks often \u2014 after every new idea, ask whether they want to\ntry one. Some students want three; some want none. Ask, don't assume.\n\n## The fill-in-the-node exercise\n\nThis is the workhorse exercise format. Show a tree with the stock prices all\nfilled in and the option values filled in everywhere except one node (and its\nancestors), then ask for two things: the missing node value, and the option\nprice today.\n\nGenerate these with the bundled script, which blanks the node you name and\nevery earlier node that depends on it, so the answer is not sitting in plain\nsight:\n\n```\npython scripts/binomial.py --S 100 --K 100 --r 0.02 --u 1.1 --d 0.9 \\\n    --n 2 --kind \"European call\" --blank 1,0 --brief\n```\n\n`--blank t,i` names the node at date `t` reached by `i` down moves, so `1,0` is\nthe up node at date 1. Paste the blanked tree to the student. Run the same\ncommand without `--blank` to get the answer for yourself before you ask.\n\n## Use the script for every number\n\n`scripts/binomial.py` prices European and American calls and puts, prints the\ntree, the risk-neutral probability, and the replicating portfolio at every node.\nRun it before you assert any value, including values you are confident about.\nBackward induction is easy to get subtly wrong in your head, and a tutor who\ntells a student their correct answer is wrong does real damage.\n\n```\npython scripts/binomial.py --S 100 --K 100 --r 0.02 --u 1.1 --d 0.9 \\\n    --n 2 --kind \"American put\"\n```\n\nThe full output includes, for each node, the value, the value of holding, the\nvalue of exercising, the hedge ratio delta, and the dollars in the bond \u2014 which\nis exactly what you need to diagnose a wrong answer. `--brief` prints the tree\nonly. `--plot trees.html` writes plotly figures of the stock and option trees;\noffer that when a student would rather see the tree than read it.\n\nConventions: `u` and `d` are gross (1.1 means +10%), `r` is per period, and\n`--d` defaults to `1/u`. If the student's numbers violate `d < 1+r < u` the\nscript refuses and explains why \u2014 that refusal is itself a good teaching moment.\n\nEvery path in this file is relative to the skill's own directory, which is not\nthe student's working directory. Resolve them against the skill folder before\nrunning or reading anything.\n\nIf Python is not available, do the arithmetic twice by two different routes\n(backward induction, and the direct risk-neutral expectation) and check they\nagree before you say anything.\n\n## Responding to an answer\n\nRight answer: confirm in one line, then push on the reasoning \u2014 \"Right. Now, if\nI told you the stock's expected return was 30% instead of 8%, what happens to\nthat price?\" Confirmation without a follow-up wastes the moment when the student\nis most receptive.\n\nWrong answer: do not give the correct number. Find where their number came from\nand ask a question that exposes it. Almost every wrong answer in this material\nis one identifiable substitution, and the number itself tells you which.\n\nWorked signatures for the running one-period example (S=100, u=1.1, d=0.9,\nr=2%, K=100, correct call price 5.88):\n\n| They said | What they did | What to ask |\n|---|---|---|\n| 6.00 | Forgot to discount | \"That's the expected payoff at date 1. Is that what you'd pay today?\" |\n| 4.90 | Used a real probability of 0.5 | \"Where did the 0.5 come from?\" |\n| 3.92 | Used 1\u2212q instead of q, or priced the put | \"Which state does your 0.4 attach to?\" |\n| 5.00 | Averaged the payoffs, no probabilities, no discounting | Both of the above |\n| 9.80 | Discounted the up payoff and ignored the down state | \"What does the option pay if the stock falls?\" |\n| 0.50 | Gave delta | \"That's the hedge ratio. What did the portfolio cost?\" |\n| 55.00 | Gave delta\u00b7S and forgot the borrowing | \"Did you pay for all of that yourself?\" |\n\nTwo of those collapse to the same number, so ask rather than assume \u2014 3.92 is\nboth the flipped-q call and the correct put.\n\nThe deepest and most common confusion is the belief that q is a forecast \u2014 that\nthe model claims the stock really has a 60% chance of going up, or that\ninvestors are risk neutral. When you see it, do not correct it with a sentence.\nGo back to the replicating portfolio: the hedge worked in both states, so no\nprobability was ever needed, and q is just the weight that makes the\nno-arbitrage answer look like an expectation. Module 2 has the full treatment.\n\nDo not praise a wrong answer, and do not soften a correction into vagueness. \"Not\nquite \u2014 check the discounting\" respects the student more than \"that's close!\"\n\n## Notation\n\nKeep it consistent across the whole session, and match the script's output:\n\n- `S` stock price, `K` strike, `r` risk-free rate per period, `u`/`d` gross up\n  and down factors, `n` periods\n- `q = (1 + r \u2212 d)/(u \u2212 d)` for the risk-neutral probability of an up move\n- Nodes named by path: `u`, `d`, `uu`, `ud`, `dd`\n- Trees drawn as one column per date, each cell `stock price / option value`,\n  exactly as the script prints them\n\nWrite trees in a fenced code block so the alignment survives.\n";</script>
```

## What Else Is in the Plugin

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-teal}
::: {.card-title}
Reference files
:::
- One teaching script per module, plus a bank of problems with verified answers
- SKILL.md names them but does not contain them --- Claude reads a module only when the student gets there
- Keeps the always-loaded instructions short and the material deep
:::
::: {.card .card-purple}
::: {.card-title}
A Python script
:::
- Prices European and American calls and puts on a tree, and reports the replicating portfolio at every node
- Claude runs it before asserting any number, so it never marks a correct answer wrong
- Can blank out a node to turn any tree into an exercise, and plot the trees

:::
:::

::: {.info-box}
[Why it is a plugin, not a prompt]{.box-title}

The tutoring protocol, the course material, and the arithmetic live in one installable package that any student can add in two commands, and that you can revise once for everyone.
:::

## Example: Agency Tutor

Business law, bundled in the same plugin (buyer beware!)

- Start a new conversation
- Enter [/tutor:agency]{.accent}

## What the Agency Tutor Does

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
::: {.card-title}
Four modules
:::
- Actual authority --- what the agent was entitled to do
- Apparent authority --- what the third party was entitled to believe
- Ratification and estoppel, when there was no authority at all
- Who pays: disclosed, unidentified, and undisclosed principals
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
::: {.card-title}
Fact patterns, not lectures
:::
- The student gets a one-paragraph problem and has to call it
- A wrong answer is diagnosed from the theory the student named, not corrected
- Runs 40--50 minutes, and stops cleanly between modules
:::
:::

## The Same Concept, Different Details

::: {.comparison-table}

| | Binomial tutor | Agency tutor |
|---|---|---|
| The student produces | A number | A theory, and a call |
| How Claude knows the answer | `binomial.py` prices the tree | `agency.py` builds the fact pattern and the answer key from the same settings |
| How a wrong answer is diagnosed | The number names the mistake | The theory named reveals the step skipped |
| The failure to guard against | Marking a correct answer wrong | Inventing a case citation |

:::


## Teaching Tool Demos {.section-divider}

## Installing the Plugins

Four plugins, one marketplace. Type each line at the Claude Code prompt.

::: {.prompt-box}
::: {.box-title}
Step 1 --- add the marketplace
:::
`/plugin marketplace add kerryback/skills`
:::

::: {.prompt-box}
::: {.box-title}
Step 2 --- install the four plugins
:::
`/plugin install voiceover@kerryback`

`/plugin install participation@kerryback`

`/plugin install poll@kerryback`

`/plugin install screenshare@kerryback`
:::

::: {.explainer}
Restart Claude after installing. Each plugin builds its own small Python environment the first time you run it, so the first launch is slower than the ones after.
:::

## Demo 1 --- Narrated Video from a Deck

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[What it does]{.card-title}

- You give it the [PDF]{.accent} of your slides --- nothing else
- Claude writes the narration; you edit any line you don't like
- ElevenLabs voices it into an `.mp4` plus a `.txt` transcript
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[What you do]{.card-title}

- Download [slide_rule.pdf](../files/session4/slide_rule.pdf){target="_blank"}
- Enter [/voiceover slide_rule.pdf]{.accent}
- Read the narration, rewrite one slide, then generate
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
Needs a free ElevenLabs API key, pasted into the banner at the top of the app. Seven slides fits inside the free monthly quota. Your students receive an mp4 to watch.
:::

## Demo 2 --- Participation from a Photo Roster

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-teal}
[What it does]{.card-title}

- Imports an ESTHER course roster PDF --- every name and headshot
- Tap 1--3 for amount and 1--3 for quality, add a note, set the date
- Save writes one row per student to `participation.csv` in the course folder
:::
::: {.card .card-purple}
[What you do]{.card-title}

- Save the roster PDF from the [Zoom chat]{.accent}, or pull your own from ESTHER
- Enter [/participation]{.accent}
- Set up a class, import the roster, score three students, open the CSV
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The sample roster is a real one, so it goes out in the chat rather than on the course site. Claude's only job is to start the app --- it launches a local web server on your machine and tells it where the PDF is. The app reads the roster itself, so the names and headshots never pass through a model and never leave your laptop.
:::

## Demo 3 --- A Live Poll on Their Phones {.shrink}

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-amber}
[What it does]{.card-title}

- Type the question as a sentence; Claude works out what kind of poll it is
- Multiple choice, word cloud, confidence scale, numeric estimate, ranking
- Anonymous by design --- no names, no roster, nothing stored per student
:::
::: {.card .card-blue}
[What you do]{.card-title}

- Enter the prompt below
- Open the student link on your own phone and answer it
- Watch the bars move on your screen
:::
:::

::: {.code-box}
/poll How confident are you using AI in your teaching? 1 to 5
:::

::: {.explainer}
Students join over an https link from a Cloudflare tunnel, so phones work on any network. Needs `cloudflared`.
:::

## Demo 4 --- Student Screens on the Projector

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-purple}
[What it does]{.card-title}

- Students open a link on their laptops, enter a name and a room code, and pick a screen, window, or tab
- You decide whose screen goes up, from a panel on the classroom computer
- Video travels [browser to browser]{.accent} --- the server only carries the handshake

:::
::: {.card .card-teal}
[What you do]{.card-title}

- Enter [/screenshare]{.accent}
- Put the display page on the projector --- join link and room code in type readable from the back row
- Share your own screen from a phone or a second laptop
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
Needs `cloudflared`, like the poll. Browsers only allow screen capture from an https page, so the tunnel is what makes this work at all --- a LAN address will fail in the room.
:::
